# Using the acceptance dynamics

With a defined simulation framework, one can begin to formulate
precisely how to use the acceptance dynamics. The core idea is
that if the bias exists or is economically relevant it should
be observable in some manner and if so we can try to minimize
the bias. Based on this hypothesis one can then formulate
a scenario, using that we have full knowledge of the applicants' population,
which allows gathering evidence on the plausibility of such hypothesis.
Having delivered this evidence, a reward signal is defined along to a formulation
of the RI problem as a reinforcement learning problem.

## Hypothesis definition (Surprise, minimization of surprise)

The most general case where we can assume unbiasedly (in the sense of this
thesis) estimated scorecards while (implicitly) ignoring the missing data
mechanism is MAR as defined on @eq-mar-only-model. Given the existence of
regularity conditions allowing for well-defined joint and marginal densities,
just like in the presented simulation framework in @sec-app-population-simulation,
the MAR condition is equivalent to
$$
Z^{(t)} \perp\!\!\!\perp Y^{:t} \big | X^{:t}
$$
from which it follows almost everywhere
$$
p_{Y | X}(y, x) = p_{Y | X, Z^{:t}=s}(y, x)
$${#eq-Y-cond-X-density-indep-Z}

with $y \in \{g, b\}, x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $s \in \{a, r\}$. If we assume

1. $N_t$ is very large, so that at each round many applicants get accepted,
2. the scorecard estimation algorithm is the same at every round, i. e.
   $\ell_t = \ell_{t'}$, $t, t' \in \mathbf{T}$, 
3. the estimation method is unbiased (in the sense of this thesis),
. the method for choosing the cut-off scoring $c_t$ remains the same
   across rounds, like choosing the validations' set optimal ROC-point and
5. A MAR missing data process

we can make an argument for the joint distribution of the accepts being
(roughly) time invariant. For lack of a better notation, this distribution
is written as $\mathbb{P}_{Y, X | Z^{(t)} = a}$ and its defined for any
measurable set $A \in 2^{E_Y} \otimes \mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}^f\right)$
as
$$
\mathbb{P}_{Y, X | Z^{(t)} = a}(A) = 
\frac{
    \mathbb{P}\left((Y, X) \in A, \hat{s}_t(X_m) > c \right)
}{
    \mathbb{P}\left(\hat{s}_t(X_m) > c \right)
}
$$

Note that this definition directly uses @eq-Z-t-with-threshold-and-scorecard-no-overwrites
by plugging in the definition of the acceptance process without overwrites,^[
    which equals the acceptance process for $f_h = 0$
] rendering it dependent on $\left(Y^{:t}, X^{:t} \right)$. Now considering that the applicants
population is time constant, for large enough $N_t$ we should expect that
each observable sample per acceptance round is roughly the same. If $\hat{s}_t$
is unbiased, then the classification should always accept applicants of the
same region of the population, as $\hat{s}_t$ would rank in a manner "alike" the
new applicants. If this happens, then the distribution of the accepts at each round
should be very alike.^[
    One could more formally say that with $\delta$ the total variation distance
    $\forall t, t' \in \mathbf{T} : \delta(\mathbb{P}_{Y, X | Z^{(t)} = a}, \mathbb{P}_{Y, X | Z^{(t')} = a}) \approx 0$
]
Given all of these conditions therefore the measured performance on the validation
set of $\hat{s}_t$ should be roughly the same as the measured rank-based performance on the
new accepts.
